processes.description: A customer or an internal originator asks for a price on gas: a fuel buyer wants to lock in volumes for future months, a municipal gas authority contact is passed along, or a colleague forwards a spreadsheet of requirements or a deal and asks whether the desk is interested. The trader prices the request against the forward curve, calls the customer back and follows up with a quote or bid.
steps: A customer or colleague sends a request for a bid, hedge or fixed forward price, often with a spreadsheet of volumes and months.
The request is routed to the trader or marketer who covers that customer, sometimes with a contact report.
The trader reviews the volumes, delivery points and term requested.
The trader prices the request against current forward prices and any transport costs.
The trader calls the customer and sends the quote or bid.
The customer accepts, declines or comes back to follow up.

stalls.summary: Requests arrive through several hands and lean on phone follow-up, so a request can wait until someone makes the call; one request asks a colleague to call the customer the same day.

automation.approach: A shared quote request form capturing customer, delivery point, months and volumes, feeding a pricing sheet that pulls current forward prices and transport adders so the trader only reviews and adjusts the number before sending a standard quote.
automation.rationale: Requests come in as free text, voice mail and spreadsheets in differing layouts; one intake and pricing layout removes the re-keying and lets the trader focus on the price decision.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round means reading the customer's volumes and months, pricing them against the forward curve and calling the customer back; around 30 minutes for a simple multi-month fixed price, more for a spreadsheet of requirements. Curve lookup and quote layout can be tooled; the price decision and the call stay manual.

processes.description: Customers, suppliers and internal desks send daily and monthly gas nominations: Calpine and Enron Methanol send standing daily nomination documents, a pipeline system sends its nomination, and plant and producer contacts send revised volumes when production drops or demand changes. Schedulers and logistics staff enter the volumes in Sitara and on the pipeline, set up the month's estimates, rework deal tickets and meters when a party revises its request, and confirm the change back.
steps: A customer, supplier or desk sends a daily or monthly nomination, or an estimate for the coming month.
The scheduler checks the volumes against the deal, meter and transport contract.
The scheduler enters or updates the volumes in Sitara and nominates them on the pipeline.
When a party revises its volumes, the scheduler updates the setup, deal ticket or meter, sometimes retroactively.
Missing transport numbers or contract details are chased with the counterparty or other desks.
The scheduler confirms the nomination is entered, tracked and balanced.

stalls.summary: Entries are reworked after mistakes or wrong files: a nomination set up wrongly at the start of the month, a spreadsheet sent empty, and a protected deal ticket that blocks correction.
Nominations wait on other parties: a transport number from another desk, and a returned phone call before a change can be confirmed; volumes sit on a temporary contract until new transport is set up.

Systems get in the way: an attachment keeps bouncing off the mail gateway, an online nomination system withdraws temporary passwords, and a counterparty asks which pipelines still accept dial-up nominations.
The same monthly setup is revised again and again within the month as volumes change, each revision re-entered by hand.

automation.approach: Parse the standing daily nomination documents and revision emails into a structured feed that pre-fills Sitara and pipeline nominations, flags changes against the prior day or month setup, and lists missing transport numbers or contracts for the scheduler to resolve.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are routine re-entry of volumes from standing documents, and the stalls come from missed checks (wrong setups, missing transport, protected tickets); a nomination checklist covering volume, meter, contract and transport before entry would cut rework tomorrow.

work_estimate.rationale: A round is checking received volumes against the deal and meter and entering them in Sitara and on the pipeline; routine daily noms take a few minutes, revisions that change setups, meters or transport contracts take longer, so about 15 minutes mid. Parsing and pre-filling routine volumes can be tooled; exceptions stay manual.

processes.description: A desk manager requests turrets, handsets, headsets, PCs and cell phones for the real-time trading group, orders are assigned to IT deployment staff who install the equipment, and the manager adjusts group calling plans and services with the carrier. Purchasing staff ask the requester to confirm receipt so the purchase can be paid, and the requisition work tends to pile up with one person.
steps: The manager or staff member requests equipment or a phone plan change.
The order is logged and assigned to an IT deployment technician.
The technician prepares and installs the equipment and reports completion.
The manager follows up with vendors or carriers on outstanding items and plan settings.
Purchasing asks the requester to confirm the items were received.
The requisition is completed so the vendor can be paid.

stalls.summary: Requests wait on vendors and installers: the manager chases a carrier on a phone for a new staff member and acknowledges that moving turrets and reconfiguring desks takes time.
Payment waits on receipt confirmation, which purchasing has to request item by item.
The purchase requisition work has no willing owner and sits with one person.
A carrier rep reverted a phone plan setting, so the change had to be made again.

contradictions.summary: Headset needs for the real-time group change: a headset is ordered urgently for one person, yet later the group is said to need no headsets.

automation.approach: A standard equipment request form routed to IT deployment, with automatic completion notices that trigger a receipt confirmation to the requester and close the requisition, plus a periodic usage report per phone plan member.
automation.rationale: The stalls are about handoffs: who owns requisitions, when receipt is confirmed, who chases vendors. A written procedure naming each owner and the receipt step addresses the ownership gap first.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work per round is placing the order or plan change with the vendor or carrier, preparing and installing the equipment, and matching receipt to the requisition; about 20 minutes mid, with installs and turret moves at the high end. One sender's remark about time spent on requisitions is a claim and does not set this.
